h1: The 6 Best Leaf Blowers for Wet Leaves of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Leaf Blowers for Wet Leaves: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six leaf blowers with the highest listed airflow for heavy, damp leaf piles, from gas backpack units to cordless handhelds.
summary: The EGO Power+ is the best leaf blower for wet leaves, with 880 CFM in a cordless handheld body. The Echo X Series offers the most airflow at 1110 CFM, but gas and a steep price limit it to big properties. PROYAMA delivers 880 CFM from a gas backpack at the lowest cost.
intro: Soaked leaves behave like a wet carpet. They mat together, stick to turf and cling to mulch, and a blower that clears a dry pile in seconds can just slide over them. In that situation the useful number is airflow volume, CFM, not the miles per hour printed in bold, because a heavy pile needs mass moved, not a thin jet.

None of the listings we reviewed promises wet-leaf performance, so this ranking works from what the specs imply. We ranked six blowers on stated CFM, power source, carry style and price bucket, accepting that more air means more weight, noise or cost. Treat the order as a spec-sheet judgment, not a promise.

products.name: EGO Power+ Cordless Electric Leaf Blower
products.verdict: 880 CFM in a handheld cordless body.
products.description:
The EGO Power+ is a cordless electric handheld with a listed 880 CFM, in the $200 to $500 bucket. There is no fuel to mix and no cord to drag.

It leads because it balances power and convenience better than anything else here. The Echo moves more air, but it is gas, backpack-carried and far more expensive. The PROYAMA matches the EGO's 880 CFM for less, though it asks you to handle fuel. For most homeowners facing damp piles, strong cordless airflow without engine upkeep is the sweet spot.

Buy it if you want serious airflow without gas. Skip it if you maintain acres and want an engine. Confirm that a battery and charger are in the box, since the listing is unclear and a battery changes the true cost considerably.
products.skipIf: You maintain acres and want gas.

products.name: Echo 220 MPH 1110 CFM 79.9 cc Gas 2-Stroke X Series Backpack Blower
products.verdict: The highest listed airflow here, at 1110 CFM and 220 MPH.
products.description:
The Echo X Series is a 79.9 cc two-stroke gas backpack blower, listed at 1110 CFM and 220 MPH, in the $500+ bucket. It is the highest airflow and the highest price in the group.

Second place reflects a steep cost for extra airflow beyond what most yards need. The EGO gets you close for far less, and the Echo adds fuel mixing, engine noise and a heavy backpack harness. Where it justifies itself is large properties with deep, soaked drifts, where its volume and speed together do real work.

Buy it for acreage, landscaping jobs or heavy leaf cover. Skip it for a regular suburban lot, where it is overkill. Plan on mixing fuel according to the manual, and expect considerably more noise than any of the cordless models.
products.idealFor: Large properties with heavy leaf cover.

products.name: PROYAMA 72CC Gas Backpack Leaf Blower
products.verdict: 880 CFM from a 72cc gas backpack in a lower bucket.
products.description:
The PROYAMA is a 72 cc gas backpack blower listed at 880 CFM, in the $100 to $200 bucket. It matches the EGO's airflow figure at a lower cost.

Third place follows from the fuel and the brand. Gas means mixing, starting and upkeep, and PROYAMA is less well known than the names around it, so support is a question mark. On paper, though, it is the cheapest way to 880 CFM here, which makes it appealing for owners who already handle gas equipment.

Buy it if you want maximum stated airflow per dollar and are comfortable with fuel. Skip it if you do not want a gas engine to maintain or if you value a major brand. Compare it against the EGO on the true cost once you factor in fuel, oil and the occasional repair.

products.name: Husqvarna 150BT Gas Leaf Blower
products.verdict: A 765 CFM gas backpack from a named outdoor brand.
products.description:
The Husqvarna 150BT is a gas backpack blower listed at 765 CFM, in the $200 to $500 bucket. It comes from an established outdoor equipment maker.

Fourth place comes from the numbers. It lists less airflow than the PROYAMA while costing more, so the brand name is what you pay for. That brings a stronger service network and a reputation for durability, which matters on a machine with an engine.

Buy it if you prefer a known maker for gas equipment and are happy with 765 CFM. Skip it if you want the most air per dollar, since the PROYAMA beats it on both counts. Check pricing against the PROYAMA before deciding, because the premium only makes sense if you value dealer support and a long track record.
products.idealFor: Buyers who prefer an established brand.
products.skipIf: You want the most airflow per dollar.

products.name: MTKOALA Leaf Blower Cordless
products.verdict: A handheld cordless blower listed at 700 CFM.
products.description:
The MTKOALA is a handheld cordless blower listed at 700 CFM, in the $100 to $200 bucket. It uses a battery, so there is no gas to deal with.

Fifth place reflects its position in the middle: less airflow than the EGO, but a lower price. For a suburban lot with moderate damp leaves, it is a sensible compromise. It will struggle more than the leaders with a thick, soaked layer, because 700 CFM leaves less margin.

Buy it for average suburban yards if you prefer cordless. Skip it if you face very heavy piles each autumn. Confirm that the battery and charger are in the box before you order, as the listing does not make that clear and a missing battery turns a bargain into an expensive tool.
products.idealFor: Suburban lots with a cordless preference.
products.skipIf: You face very heavy leaf piles.

products.name: LOSART Leaf Blower Cordless
products.verdict: A 650 CFM cordless blower in a low bucket.
products.description:
The LOSART is a cordless blower listed at 650 CFM, in the $50 to $100 bucket. It is the lowest airflow and among the lowest prices in this ranking.

It closes the list because 650 CFM gives the least margin on soaked leaves, and the brand offers little support. Even so, it is a legitimate tool for a small yard, and it avoids fuel entirely. If you clear damp leaves in small batches, it can do the job slowly.

Buy it for small yards and light, damp cleanup. Skip it if you need to move heavy piles in a single pass. Expect to work in smaller sections, and treat the 650 CFM figure as a ceiling on what the tool can do against wet material, not a promise.
products.skipIf: You need to move heavy piles.

whatMatters.detail: CFM counts cubic feet of air per minute leaving the nozzle. Heavy damp piles need volume to shift, so this figure matters more than speed. Find it in the title or bullets. The range here runs from 650 CFM on the LOSART to 1110 CFM on the Echo.

MPH is air speed at the nozzle. It helps pry stuck leaves off turf but cannot move a pile on its own. Use it as a tie-breaker after CFM. The Echo lists 220 MPH, but most listings here omit speed entirely, so compare CFM first.

Gas gives long runtime and big airflow but needs fuel, maintenance and tolerance for noise. Cordless is quieter and simpler, but limited by battery. Check the power source in the title and what comes in the box. The Echo, PROYAMA and Husqvarna are gas, and the EGO, MTKOALA and LOSART are cordless.

A backpack spreads the weight across your shoulders and hips, which suits long sessions, while handhelds are lighter for short jobs. Match the style to your yard and your back. The Echo, PROYAMA and Husqvarna are backpacks, and the EGO and MTKOALA are handhelds.

A listing without a CFM figure is hard to compare, and we treat that gap with caution. We left the Husqvarna 360BT out of the ranking for this reason. Always find a stated airflow before you trust a blower to move a heavy wet pile.

faq.q: What CFM do I need for wet leaves?
faq.a: No listing gives a wet-leaf figure, so choose the highest stated CFM that fits your budget and carry preference. The EGO's 880 CFM is the best balance, while the Echo's 1110 CFM suits large properties.
Buying on MPH alone. Airflow volume does more work on heavy damp piles. The Echo's 220 MPH is impressive, but CFM tells you how much material the blower can actually push.

faq.q: Is the Echo worth it over the EGO?
faq.a: Only on large properties. The EGO lists 880 CFM and costs far less, so for most yards the Echo's extra air does not justify the fuel, weight and price.

faq.q: How do I start a gas backpack?
faq.a: Mix fuel exactly as the manual directs and follow the start steps. Do not guess the ratio. The PROYAMA, Husqvarna and Echo are gas backpacks, so read the starting instructions before the first use.
Keep air filters clean and follow the manual for storage and fuel. Cordless models like the EGO need clear vents and a battery stored indoors, while gas units need regular filter and plug checks.

faq.q: Can a cordless blower handle wet piles?
faq.a: On paper, yes: the EGO lists 880 CFM. Expect shorter runtime on a heavy pile, and consider a spare battery if your yard is large.

finalTake: For most yards facing wet leaves, the EGO Power+ is the blower to buy, with 880 CFM and no engine to maintain. Choose the Echo X Series only for acreage and heavy drifts, or the PROYAMA if you want the cheapest gas option at the same stated airflow. Read the CFM first and the miles per hour second.
